title: Benjamin and the Family of Saul
summary: The chapter returns to Benjamin in fuller detail than chapter 7, listing its clans, their towns, and the families who lived in Jerusalem and Gibeon. It ends with the family of Saul, Israel's first king, traced from his grandfather Ner through Jonathan and Merib-baal for many generations, down to a clan of Benjaminite archers.
story: Chapter 7 gave Benjamin a few verses among the northern tribes. Now the Chronicler gives the tribe a whole chapter, for two reasons. Benjamin, with Judah and Levi, formed the core of the kingdom of Judah after the north broke away, and Benjaminites were among those who returned from exile (Ezra 1:5). And Benjamin was the tribe of Saul, whose death opens the story of David in chapter 10. The chapter ends by setting Saul's family before the reader, and it does so without comment. Saul's line did not die with him. Through Jonathan and his son Merib-baal it continued for more than ten generations, into a large clan of warriors. The house that lost the throne was not wiped out.
historical:
Benjamin's territory was small but strategic, lying between Judah and Ephraim just north of Jerusalem, and the towns named here reflect that: Geba, Gibeon, Aijalon, and Jerusalem itself (verse 28), which sat on the border between Benjamin and Judah. Ono and Lod (verse 12) lay further west, near the coastal plain, and both appear among the towns resettled after the exile (Ezra 2:33; Nehemiah 11:35). The note about Beriah and Shema driving out the inhabitants of Gath (verse 13) suggests Benjaminite clashes with the Philistines. Ehud (verse 6) may be the left-handed judge of Judges 3:15, who was a Benjaminite and a descendant of Gera.

Saul reigned as Israel's first king in the late eleventh century BC. His sons Jonathan, Malchishua, and Abinadab died with him at Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2), as chapter 10 will tell. Esh-baal is the son called Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel 2 to 4, who reigned briefly over the northern tribes after Saul's death. Merib-baal is Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, lame from childhood, to whom David showed kindness for Jonathan's sake (2 Samuel 4:4; 9).
cultural:
Two of the names in Saul's family, Esh-baal and Merib-baal, contain the word baal, which in Hebrew means lord or master and was also the name of the Canaanite storm god. In Saul's time it seems to have been used as a title for the LORD himself, without any intent to honor the Canaanite god. Later, when Baal worship had become Israel's great temptation, the books of Samuel as we have them replaced baal in these names with bosheth, which means shame, giving Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth. Chronicles preserves the older forms. Hosea 2:16-17 shows the same unease with the word: God says his people will no longer call him my Baal.

The skill of Benjaminite fighters was famous. Judges 20:16 describes left-handed Benjaminite slingers who could hit a hair without missing, and 1 Chronicles 12:2 describes Benjaminite archers who could shoot and sling with either hand. The descendants of Ulam in verse 40 carry that reputation. The phrase many sons and grandsons marks a clan that had grown strong, a sign of blessing in the ancient world.
literary: The chapter is a segmented genealogy organized by places more than by strict family lines. It begins with Benjamin's sons (verses 1 to 5), then moves through clusters of families tied to Geba, Moab, Ono and Lod, Aijalon, and Jerusalem (verses 6 to 28), each cluster closing with a note about where they lived or what they did. The Gibeon section (verses 29 to 40) then leads into the family of Saul, which runs as a linear list for many generations before ending in a burst of numbers and warriors. The whole of verses 29 to 38 is repeated with minor differences in 9:35-44, where it leads straight into the story of Saul's death. The repetition works like a hinge: the reader meets Saul's family once as part of Benjamin and again as the doorway into the narrative.

outline.t: Benjamin's sons and the family of Bela
The families of Geba and the descendants of Shaharaim
Benjaminite clans of Aijalon and Jerusalem
The family of Jeiel of Gibeon
The family of Saul through Jonathan to the archers of Ulam

doctrines.note: Saul lost the kingdom, and his sons died with him in battle, yet his line through Jonathan continued for generations. God's judgment on Saul's reign did not mean the destruction of his family, and the chapter records that survival without fanfare.

The names Esh-baal and Merib-baal, later changed in Samuel to forms using the word for shame, show how Israel's language itself was affected by the struggle against Baal worship. Words that once served could later carry a danger.

words.note: Merib-baal, the name of Jonathan's son. It probably means the lord contends or champion of the lord. In 2 Samuel he is Mephibosheth, with baal replaced by bosheth, shame. Chronicles keeps the original name, which suggests that in Saul's day baal could be used as a title for the LORD.

Saul, meaning asked for. The name recalls the people's demand for a king in 1 Samuel 8. The Chronicler places Saul's family at the end of Benjamin's genealogy so that the reader knows who he is before the narrative of his death begins in chapter 10.

Galah, to go into exile or be carried away (verse 6). Even within the tribal genealogies, the Chronicler notes displacements and exiles, reminding his readers that being uprooted was part of Israel's history long before Babylon.

Qeshet, bow. The descendants of Ulam were archers (verse 40). The bow was a key weapon in ancient warfare, and Benjaminite skill with it was well known; in 1 Chronicles 12:2 Benjaminite archers come over to David.

christ: Saul's family line continues through Jonathan, David's covenant friend, and through Merib-baal, whom David brought to his table and treated like one of his own sons (2 Samuel 9). That act of kindness to the grandson of a rival king is one of the most striking pictures of grace in the Old Testament. The New Testament does not directly apply it to Christ, so any link is thematic, but readers have long seen in it a pattern of the gospel: a king who welcomes those from a fallen house, who could claim nothing, to eat at his table. Paul, who was himself from the tribe of Benjamin and bore the Hebrew name Saul, like his tribe's most famous son (Philippians 3:5; Acts 13:9, 21), became one of the great witnesses to that grace.

hard.q: Why did Saul's family have names containing Baal, and why were the names changed in Samuel?
hard.a: The Hebrew word baal is an ordinary noun meaning owner, lord, or husband, and it was also the title of the leading Canaanite god. Many scholars think that in Saul's day Israelites could use baal as a title for the LORD, so that Esh-baal meant something like man of the lord, with no intention of honoring the Canaanite deity. Others think the names show that Canaanite religion had influenced even Saul's household. Later, when the prophets were fighting the worship of Baal, the word became so tainted that writers avoided it. The books of Samuel, as they have come down to us, replace baal with bosheth (shame), giving Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth. Whether the authors of Samuel or later copyists made the change is debated. Chronicles preserves the older forms, which suggests that the Chronicler drew on records, or a text of Samuel, from before the change was made.

questions: Saul's line continued long after his failure. What does this suggest about how God's judgment and God's mercy can both be at work in the same family?
The word baal was once used innocently but later became dangerous. Are there habits or words in your life that were once harmless but now lead you away from God?
David showed kindness to Saul's grandson, who had no claim on him. Who might you welcome to your table who can give you nothing in return?
